title: Banjoists Amy Sharp and Buzzy, and the Mummers-style banjo bands
summary: Jones praises Amy Sharp's rhythm banjo and Buzzy's technique, and they discuss how the old mummers banjo bands turned from playing tunes to sing-along schtick.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: And you never got out your old banjo in March.
Do you know Amy Sharp did not know what the Mummers were? We had to explain it. In fact, she thought we were putting her on for the longest time. Where is she from, Philadelphia?
Oh, yeah. She didn't know what a Mummers band was.

Yeah. You use her how often now? Right now she's working three days a week. While Buzzy was out during the summer with the center stage or whatever it is. She was working six days a week for about two months.
Is she a strong banjo player would you say?

I'll tell you what, she's a good banjo player for what I need as any I've ever had. She's not strong as far as power, sheer power. But then again I don't have a powerful band, I don't have a loud band. But she's one of the best rhythm banjo players that I've ever heard in my life. And how long has she been playing? She's only been playing about three years, totally. She just has that knack, Richard. And the longer she plays the better she will get. She's one of those kind of people who just started late in life. Most people who start that late in life never seem to develop, but she did. She's fortunate. And then Buzzy's something else. Buzzy's a harder player than she is and he's got more technique and a larger repertoire. But then again Buzzy's fifteen years older than she is too.
Well fifteen years old and he's been playing for more than three years. Yeah. And he's been... Probably since he was a kid.

Buzzy started when he was a senior in high school. Amy started when she was a sophomore in college. But Buzzy has the added advantage of having played with your father's mustache bands back when they first started. Which at that time wasn't the hoopla and all the BS that it is. Now they did mostly tunes. They were background music at that time. They did tunes and he learned chord changes and learned how to play rhythm banjo behind a lead banjo player. Now they don't do tunes? Well they do schtick now. They sing alongs and whoopies and hooplas and all that crap. You know it's loud. Get the audience frenzied up and drinking beer and stomping their feet and everything. That's what it developed to a good time whoopie parlor.

I've never have been to one in so many years. See the times I've been to them, although I didn't always like what they were doing, I always respected the musicianship of those players. They were good players.
They had some awfully fine players.
Yeah, I'm talking about the people that say would be playing with Jay Brackett. And of course Les Muscat was working on them.
Jimmy Hazelup. Oh, quite a few good players. Good and agile players.
